title: GenAI Interview Playbook
blurb: The 23-week plan from Oct 26 2026 to Mar 31 2027: Python and SQL, LLM and RAG internals, agents, production, system design and mocks, each week ending in a proof artifact.
audience: Software engineers preparing for AI engineer interviews

tracks.title: Foundations
tracks.blurb: Role targeting, Python, SQL, ML and LLM basics, prompting and API patterns.

tracks.title: RAG
tracks.blurb: Embeddings, RAG architecture, debugging and evaluation.

tracks.title: Agents
tracks.blurb: Bounded agents, orchestration, MCP, reliability and security.

tracks.title: Production and design
tracks.blurb: LLMOps, deployment and AI system design.

tracks.title: Interview loop
tracks.blurb: Resume, mock loops, full simulations and the toolkit.

sections.title: Positioning, Python and SQL (Oct 26 to Nov 22)

nodes.title: Week 1 · Baseline + positioning (Oct 26 to Nov 1)
nodes.summary: Choose 3 role families; collect 10 job descriptions; baseline Python, SQL and DSA mock; record current gaps. Proof artifact: Role matrix + gap tracker. Decode each JD into must-have versus nice-to-have skills, write a one-sentence position you can defend, and re-run the baseline mocks after week five so the gap tracker moves with evidence rather than mood.

nodes.title: Week 2 · Python coding round (Nov 2 to Nov 8)
nodes.summary: Strings, dict/set, functions, exceptions, typing; solve small coding tasks without IDE autocomplete. Proof artifact: 10 Python exercises + review notes. Practise without autocomplete, narrate complexity before you type, and keep an error log that a later week can re-open. The bar is a function you can test on empty and huge inputs and explain in ninety seconds.

nodes.title: Week 3 · Python backend round (Nov 9 to Nov 15)
nodes.summary: OOP, modules, testing, logging, HTTP, async/await, error handling. Proof artifact: Mini API walkthrough. Treat the mini API as something you would on-call: timeouts, validation, retries with jitter, structured logs, and tests that do not hit the network. Be ready to walk an interviewer through one failure path. Walk one incident path: timeout, replayed write, and the log field you would grep.

nodes.title: Week 4 · SQL + data systems (Nov 16 to Nov 22)
nodes.summary: Joins, CTEs, window functions, indexes, transactions, schema design. Proof artifact: Timed SQL set + explained query plans. Every query you keep must have a plan you can defend, and the schema must express tenant and permission so a later RAG filter is not a hope. Practise saying isolation levels with a race, not a slogan.

sections.title: ML, neural nets and LLM foundations (Nov 23 to Dec 20)

nodes.title: Week 5 · ML fundamentals (Nov 23 to Nov 29)
nodes.summary: Train/test split, leakage, overfitting, metrics, vectors, probability and linear models. Proof artifact: Explain 15 ML questions. Interviewers want leakage, whether the metric matches the decision, and a linear model you can still explain if the deep-net story falls apart. Fifteen questions only count if they are spoken without notes.

nodes.title: Week 6 · Neural nets + PyTorch (Nov 30 to Dec 6)
nodes.summary: Tensors, gradients, loss, optimization; compare training and inference. Proof artifact: Explain a simple training loop. Be able to narrate one training step, separate train from infer, and say where memory goes as the sequence grows. A bigger net is not the first fix for overfitting. Print a tensor shape after flatten; say what zero-grad prevents; keep one overfit story with the first two fixes.

sections.title: Embeddings, RAG and evaluation (Dec 21 to Jan 17)

nodes.summary: Embedding model choice, similarity, chunking, metadata and pgvector. Proof artifact: Retrieval prototype. Retrieval quality starts with what you embed, which ids you store, and whether keyword still wins for codes and names. Filters belong in the query, not in a later Python loop that already leaked scores.

nodes.title: Week 10 · RAG architecture (Dec 28 to Jan 3)
nodes.summary: Ingestion, retrieval, context construction, citations, access control and abstention. Proof artifact: RAG architecture diagram. Draw ingest to cited answer with an empty-retrieval policy and tenant isolation that does not live in the prompt. Freshness needs a content hash, not only a cron. Name the bound on prompt size, the citation path, and who is blocked when retrieval is empty. Do not put.

nodes.title: Week 11 · RAG debugging (Jan 4 to Jan 10)
nodes.summary: BM25 vs dense, hybrid search, reranking, chunking failures, query rewriting. Proof artifact: Failure analysis report. Debug by stage with replayable ids, not by raising top_k. A failure report that cannot name the retrieved chunks is not a report. Inspect query, retrieved ids, prompt and output in the first fifteen minutes. Prefer a chunk, hybrid or refuse fix over a larger top_k.

sections.title: Agents, orchestration and security (Jan 18 to Feb 7)

nodes.title: Week 13 · Agent fundamentals (Jan 18 to Jan 24)
nodes.summary: Agent vs workflow, tool schema, state, stopping conditions, error handling. Proof artifact: Bounded tool-using agent. An agent you can defend has a schema, a budget, a stop rule, and a tool you can stub. If the steps are known, say so and use a workflow. Trigger the step budget and the stop rule on purpose once, and be ready to say when a fixed workflow is the better design.

nodes.title: Week 14 · Agent orchestration + MCP (Jan 25 to Jan 31)
nodes.summary: Stateful graphs, checkpoints, human approval, MCP concepts and tool permissions. Proof artifact: Agent workflow diagram + demo. Durability means a crash does not resend a side effect. MCP is a way to expose tools; you still choose the servers and the permissions. A restart must not resend an email or a refund. Approval is a durable event; MCP does not replace your allow-list.

nodes.title: GenAI system design framework
nodes.summary: The eight-step design framework and five practice scenarios. The eight steps are a spine you can skip when the interviewer already locked a step. Spend leftover time on the risk, not on a prettier second diagram. Write requirements and a rough QPS before the vector database. One named-variable cost pass beats a second unused diagram. Practise one full scenario and stop after the risk you would.
checklist: Read the lesson: GenAI system design: the 8-step interview framework
Apply it in your next weekly review: genai system design framework
Write down what you changed after using it once
Time a 20-minute design using the eight steps and note which step you under-served
Do one back-of-envelope cost or latency pass with named variables, not invented precision
List what you would cut if the budget or the latency SLO dropped by 10x

nodes.title: Project deep-dive template
nodes.summary: How to tell a project story like an engineer, plus the five-minute demo structure. Rehearse until the five-minute demo is five minutes and the hard follow-ups have true answers. Contribution, eval, and a cut list matter more than the stack. Own your part in one sentence a teammate would recognise. Point at the eval file, and name one stage you would delete if the metric did not move.
checklist: Read the lesson: Project deep-dive template: structure, demo script, honest follow-ups
Apply it in your next weekly review: project deep-dive template
Write down what you changed after using it once
Time a five-minute demo that shows one success, one citation or trace, and one handled miss
Write answers to 'what did you own?' and 'what would you delete?' that a teammate would recognise
Point at the eval file or score table you would open if asked for evidence

nodes.title: STAR-L story bank
nodes.summary: Six to eight truthful behavioural stories with Situation, Task, Action, Result and Learning. Six to eight true stories that cover ownership, conflict, failure and prioritisation, each with a result and a learning. Dates must survive a resume check. Cover ownership, conflict, failure and prioritisation. Drop slogan learnings and any story you would not repeat in front of a teammate.
checklist: Read the lesson: STAR-L story bank for behavioural interviews
Apply it in your next weekly review: star-l story bank
Write down what you changed after using it once
Write or tighten six STAR-L cards and read two of them aloud to a timer
Check every story against resume dates and drop any you would not repeat in front of a teammate
Add one learning you have actually reused; delete slogan learnings

nodes.title: Readiness gates and weekly score
nodes.summary: Eight readiness gates and the Sunday 0-5 score that decides next week's focus. Score from evidence, save the sheet, and let 2s set the next week. Applying while core gates sit at 1 is a choice you should say out loud, not a default. A 4 needs an artifact or a scored mock you can point at. Turn every 2 into a named Tuesday drill and save the sheet so the trend is visible.
checklist: Read the lesson: Readiness Gates and Weekly Scoring
Apply it in your next weekly review: readiness gates and weekly score
Write down what you changed after using it once
Save a Sunday 0-5 sheet with a one-line evidence note under each domain
Turn every score of 2 or below into a named drill on the next week's plan
Refuse to mark a gate at 4 without an artifact or a scored mock you can point at

nodes.title: Stretch: GPU serving and Kubernetes
nodes.summary: AI platform roles may ask about model serving and orchestration. Treat this as optional: learn it only if your target job descriptions repeat it. Only if three or more target JDs repeat serving or Kubernetes: learn the trade-off between a managed endpoint and an open-weight server, and what a probe checks. Otherwise leave it.
checklist: Check whether 3 or more target job descriptions list GPU serving or Kubernetes
If yes, read the open-weight serving lesson and note the vLLM or TGI serving trade-offs
If no, leave it and spend the time on a core weak domain
If the JD bar is met, note batching, KV-cache and paged-attention as serving ideas you can explain without deploying them
Write liveness versus readiness for a model server in two sentences
If the JD bar is not met, write that decision in the tracker and put the hours on a weak core domain

nodes.title: Supplemental: fine-tuning a small model
nodes.summary: The playbook asks you to know when fine-tuning beats prompting or RAG. Building one is optional unless a job description asks for it. Know the decision: prompting, RAG, longer context, or fine-tuning. Building a LoRA is optional unless a JD requires it, and it still needs an eval against a prompt baseline.
checklist: Be able to explain when to use prompting, RAG, fine-tuning or a longer context window
Read the lesson on LoRA, QLoRA and PEFT
Only if a target role needs it: run one small LoRA fine-tune and evaluate against a prompt baseline
Give a closed-book rule for when fine-tuning is the wrong first move versus RAG or a better prompt
Read the LoRA/QLoRA lesson and write three bullets on rank, memory and what data you would need
If a target role requires it, run one small LoRA and compare it to a frozen-prompt baseline on the same set
